As of 304 AM Saturday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... The remnants of Isaias will bring periods of 
showers through Sunday. A threat of severe thunderstorms capable of 
tornadoes will also exist Sunday.

The remnants of Isaias are presently located some 50 miles south-
southwest of Montgomery AL. Over the next 24-36 hours, most model 
and ensemble guidance is in good agreement in tracking the remnants 
of Isaias from east-central AL today into the eastern TN valley by 
early Sunday. From Sunday onward, the extratropical system will 
occlude and weaken as it tracks ENE south of New England by early 
Monday.

Rainfall expectations: There has not been much change with the 
latest guidance with respect to rainfall totals. The latest 00z 
HREF/REFS are in relatively good agreement on precipitation totals, 
ranging from 0.75 inches to 2 inches. Amounts are expected to be 
highest across the far NW Piedmont/Triad, where upslope may combine 
with isentropic ascent, as well as over the Coastal Plain where 
instability will come into play. A pocket of lower rainfall totals 
may exist over the Triangle and central portions of the area, with 
some spots potentially seeing a half inch or less. Of course, 
embedded higher rainfall totals are possible anywhere in central NC, 
especially Sunday when convective chances greatly increase within 
the very moist tropical-like airmass. Periods of showers will exist 
today and tonight, but there will certainly be times of dry weather, 
especially the early part of the day when dry air will exist in the 
low-levels.

Wind gusts: An increasing pressure gradient will develop today with 
a retreating high to our northeast and the remnants of Isaias moving 
northeastward. Wind gusts out of the ENE will range from 25-30 mph, 
with infrequent gusts upwards of 35 mph across the west and southern 
Piedmont. These gusts should weaken later tonight in the 15-25 mph 
range as the gradient gradually relaxes. Under a developing CAD 
wedge today, highs will range from the low/mid 60s NW to low 70s SE.

Severe threat: Probably the most concerning aspect to this weekend 
system is the threat of severe weather. The latest update from SPC 
indicates a category increase in the severe weather risk, especially 
for Sunday. The Marginal Risk has expanded for late tonight and 
early Sunday across the southern Piedmont, Sandhills, Central 
Coastal Plain, and far southern areas of the Triangle. On Sunday, 
there is now a Slight Risk in place for all but the far western 
Piedmont of central NC.

Based on model fields, it would appear the chance of severe storms 
will be rather limited for most of Saturday. The better chance of 
some isolated severe storms will exist after midnight tonight and 
prior to daybreak Sun, when lower 70s dewpoints spread northward 
within an increasingly sheared environment. Confidence is not great 
on coverage for this early Sunday period given a lack of storm 
coverage shown in high-res guidance.

The better chance of severe weather should be from mid-morning 
Sunday into early Sunday evening. During this time, a secondary low 
will form across the NW Piedmont along the CAD boundary/warm front. 
As the low tracks ENE into VA during the day, low to mid 70s 
dewpoints will spread over most of the region. A southwesterly low-
level jet of 40-45 kts will be in place, along with dewpoints in the 
low/mid 70s in an increasing warm sector. The 00z HREF/REFS indicate 
a corridor of strong instability of 1200-1500 J/kg as a dry slot 
steepens lapse rates across central and eastern areas of the Slight 
Risk zone. A strengthening low and deep-layer shear profile will 
support transient supercells with the threat for a brief tornado or 
two and damaging wind gusts. The 00z HREF/REFS and HRRR show a 
signal for a broken band of convection moving through the early 
afternoon to early evening along and east of the Triad. While 
uncertainty remains, things are certainly concerning for Sunday.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Much of next week will be unseasonably warm, with 
very little to no chance of rain.

Broad mid/upper ridging over the Southeastern US will bring mostly 
sunny and dry weather to central NC from Monday through Friday of 
next week. Any troughing will be confined to the Western and 
Northeastern US. One of those shortwaves (and associated area of 
surface low pressure) will move across the Great Lakes and New 
England on Tuesday into early Wednesday, dropping a backdoor cold 
front south into the Mid-Atlantic. This front will be moisture-
starved so there will most likely be no precipitation with it, and 
if there is any it would be very light, with even the 90th 
percentile of ensemble guidance less than a tenth of an inch. A 
northern stream shortwave will dive down from Canada late in the 
week and potentially interact with the Western US trough, which
